en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 18.
Vattakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Duties)
1. Discussion on the Duties for Visitors.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, visiting monks entered the monastery even while wearing sandals, and even while holding up sunshades.
They entered the monastery; they entered the monastery even with their heads covered; they entered the monastery even with their robes placed over their heads;
they washed their feet with drinking water; they did not pay homage to the resident monks who were senior, nor did they inquire about the lodgings.
Furthermore, a certain visiting monk, having turned up the latch and pushed open the door, entered the dwelling hastily, even though it was already occupied.
A snake fell upon his back from above.
Terrified, he let out a cry.
The monks ran up and said this to that monk:
“Friend, why did you raise such a cry?
Then that bhikkhu reported the matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“How can incoming bhikkhus enter the monastery wearing sandals, enter the monastery holding a sunshade,
enter the monastery with their heads covered, enter the monastery with their robes draped over their heads,
wash their feet with drinking water, and fail to pay homage to the resident bhikkhus who are senior?”
“Nor will they ask about the lodgings.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [and so on] … “Is it true,
bhikkhus, that visiting bhikkhus enter the monastery even with their sandals on, and even while holding up a sunshade?”
“They enter the monastery; they enter the monastery even with their heads covered; they enter the monastery even with their robes draped over their heads;
they wash their feet with drinking water; and they do not pay homage to the resident monks who are senior, nor do they inquire about the lodgings.
“Is this true, Blessed One? “It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One,
rebuked them: “… How can it be, monks, that visiting monks enter the monastery wearing sandals, enter the monastery holding umbrellas,
enter the monastery with their heads covered, or even enter the monastery having placed their robes on their heads?”
“They will enter [the dwelling], they will wash their feet with drinking water, and they will neither pay homage to the more senior resident monks nor inquire about their lodgings.
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... Having rebuked them... [the Buddha said:]”
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Therefore, bhikkhus, I shall lay down the proper conduct for incoming bhikkhus, as it should be correctly observed by incoming bhikkhus.
An incoming bhikkhu, thinking, ‘Now I will enter the monastery,’ should remove his sandals and set them down low.”
Having done so, having shaken [the robe], having taken it up, having lowered the sunshade, having uncovered the head, and having placed the upper robe over the shoulder,
one should enter the monastery carefully and without haste.
As one enters the monastery, one should take note:
‘Where do the resident monks withdraw?’—
wherever the resident monks withdraw:
whether in the assembly hall, or in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree.
Having gone there, one should set down one’s bowl to one side;
one’s robe should be set down to one side;
and having taken a suitable seat, one should sit down.
One should ask for drinking water and one should ask for water for washing:
"Which is the drinking water? Which is the water for washing?
If there is need for drinking water, one should take the drinking water and drink it.
If there is need for refreshments, one should take refreshments and wash the feet.
While washing the feet, water should be poured with one hand and the feet washed with the other.
One should not pour the water with the same hand as the one used to wash the feet.
Having asked for a cloth for wiping sandals, the sandals should be wiped.
When wiping the sandals, one should first wipe them with a dry cloth and afterwards with a damp one.
Having washed the cloth for wiping sandals, it should be hung aside.
If the resident monk is senior, he should be saluted;
if he is junior, he should be made to salute.
One should ask about his lodging: "Which lodging has been assigned to me?"
One should ask whether it has been inhabited or not; one should ask about the proper range for alms-gathering and the improper range;
one should ask about families designated as "in training"; one should ask about the place for defecating and the place for urinating;
one should ask about drinking water and bathing water; one should ask about a walking stick; [and one should ask] for the Saṅgha...
The agreement should be asked:
“At what time should one enter, and at what time should one leave?
If the dwelling has not been inhabited, one should knock on the door, wait for a moment, lift the bolt, open the door, and look inside while standing outside.
If the dwelling is dirty—if a bed has been placed upon a bed, or a bench upon a bench, or the bedding has been piled on top—then if one is able, it should be cleaned.
While cleaning the dwelling, first the floor-covering should be taken out and set aside;
the bed-legs should be taken out and set aside.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having removed the sitting mat and the rug, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should carry it out to one side, being careful not to strike it or to jolt the door-panel.
Having lowered the seat, one should take it out and place it to one side, doing so carefully without scraping it or knocking against the surface of the door-panel.
The spittoon should be taken out and placed to one side;
the leaning board should be taken out and placed to one side.
If there is mold on the dwelling, it should first be removed from the ceiling; the light openings, joints, and corners should be wiped clean.
If a wall treated with red ocher has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the floor treated with black pigment has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has not been prepared, it should be sprinkled with water and swept, thinking:
"Lest the dwelling be covered in dust.
Having cleared away the refuse, it should be thrown aside to one side.
The floor-covering should be dried in the sun, cleaned, beaten to remove dust, brought back inside, and spread out in its proper place.
The bed-legs should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and set down in their proper place.

The bed should be dried in the sun, cleaned, beaten to remove dust, lowered, and then carefully brought back inside—without scraping it against the floor or knocking it against the door frame—and spread out in its proper place.

Having aired out the seat, cleaned it, and dusted it, having lowered it and carefully avoided scraping it or knocking against the surface of the door-panel, one should carry it back and arrange it in its proper place.
Having aired out the mattress and pillow, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should carry them back and arrange them according to their respective parts.
Having aired out the sitting mat and the rug, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should carry them back and arrange them according to their respective parts.
The spittoon, having been rinsed, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place.
The leaning board, having been rinsed, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes should be put away.
When setting down the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the base of the bed or the base of the chair before setting the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on bare ground.

When setting down the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand and, with the other hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string; then, having arranged the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, the robe should be set down.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If the southern winds blow with dust, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night.
If it is hot, the windows should be closed during the day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If there is no drinking water, drinking water should be provided.
"If there is no food for consumption, food for consumption should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water should be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
This, monks, is the duty for visiting monks, and it is how visiting monks should conduct themselves properly."

2. Discussion on the Duties of Resident Monks Now at that time, when resident monks saw incoming monks, they neither prepared a seat for them, nor set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, or a foot-washing stone;
nor did they go out to meet them to receive their bowls and robes.
They accepted [the offerings], yet they did not inquire after their water; nor did they pay homage to the visiting monks who were senior, nor did they prepare lodgings for them.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:

“How can it be that resident bhikkhus, upon seeing visiting bhikkhus, neither prepare a seat, nor set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone; nor go forth to meet them and receive their bowls and robes;
nor ask them if they want drinking water; nor even pay homage to visiting bhikkhus who are senior?”

“They will not assign lodgings. Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that …? … [as before] … “It is true, Blessed One. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, this is neither suitable for me nor fitting, that my disciples should not assign lodgings. … [as before] … “Therefore, bhikkhus, I allow you to assign lodgings. … [as before] … “How, bhikkhus, should lodgings be assigned? Lodgings should be assigned by way of seniority. But when a new dwelling arises, it should be assigned to whoever arrives first. This is the rule. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of seniority. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it may be assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of seniority. There are these five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of seniority. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another.

(3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it is assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of seniority. Therefore, bhikkhus, I allow you to assign lodgings by way of seniority. But when a new dwelling arises, it should be assigned to whoever arrives first. This is the rule. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it may be assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival. There are these five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it is assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival. Therefore, bhikkhus, I allow you to assign lodgings by way of arrival. But when a new dwelling arises, it should be assigned to whoever arrives first. This is the rule. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it may be assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. There are these five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it is assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. Therefore, bhikkhus, I allow you to assign lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. But when a new dwelling arises, it should be assigned to whoever arrives first. This is the rule. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it may be assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. There are these five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it is assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. Therefore, bhikkhus, I allow you to assign lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. But when a new dwelling arises, it should be assigned to whoever arrives first. This is the rule. … [as before] … “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early may be ill; his bed and chair may be taken away from him and given to another. (5) When a new dwelling arises, it may be assigned to whoever arrives first. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. There are these five advantages in assigning lodgings by way of arrival even for a new dwelling. What five? (1) A bhikkhu who is senior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (2) A bhikkhu who is junior and ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (3) A bhikkhu who has arrived late and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another. (4) A bhikkhu who has arrived early and is ill does not have to move from his bed and chair to another.
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
… Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for resident monks, showing how resident monks should behave correctly.
When a resident monk sees an incoming monk who is senior, he should prepare a seat;
he should set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone; and having gone out to meet him, he should take his bowl and robe.”
It should be accepted; he should be asked for water.
If he is able, his sandals should be wiped.
When wiping the sandals, they should first be wiped with a dry cloth and afterwards with a wet one.
Having washed the foot-wiping cloth, it should be set aside to one side.
An incoming bhikkhu who is senior should be saluted.
A lodging should be prepared for him.
‘This dwelling place falls to you.
Whether it has been already occupied or not, it should be pointed out.
The alms-round should be pointed out.
The improper range should be pointed out.
Families designated as "for those in training" should be pointed out.
The place for defecation should be pointed out.
The place for urination should be pointed out.
Drinking water should be pointed out.
Water for washing should be pointed out.
The staff-bearer should be instructed.
The Sangha’s agreement on the form of conduct should be announced:
"At this time one should enter; at this time one should depart."
If he is a junior, he should point it out while remaining seated:
"Place your bowl here; place your robe here; sit on this seat.
He should also point out the drinking water.
The articles for personal use must be pointed out.
The cloth for wiping sandals must be pointed out.
A newly arrived junior monk must be made to pay respects.
The lodging should be pointed out, saying:
“This lodging falls to you.
It should be pointed out whether it has been already occupied or not yet occupied.
The proper resort should be explained;
the improper resort should be explained;
families designated as "for those in training" should be explained.
The place for defecation should be pointed out.
The place for urination should be pointed out.
Drinking water should be pointed out.
The utensils for use should be pointed out.
A walking staff should be pointed out.
The Sangha’s agreement on boundaries should be pointed out.
‘One should enter at this time; one should depart at this time.
This, monks, is the duty for resident monks, the way in which resident monks should conduct themselves properly.
3. Discussion on the Duties of Those Going on a Journey.

Now at that time, monks who were traveling away departed without putting away their wooden and earthenware utensils, without closing the doors and windows, and without informing [the resident] regarding the lodgings.
Consequently, the wooden and earthenware utensils were lost,
and the lodgings remained unprotected.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these departing monks depart without putting away their wooden and earthenware utensils, without closing the doors and windows, and without informing the resident on the lodging?
The wooden and earthenware utensils are being lost!"
“The lodging is unprotected.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that … [as before] …?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
… Having rebuked him … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Therefore, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for monks who are traveling, so that traveling monks may conduct themselves correctly.
A monk who is traveling, monks, having put away his wooden and ceramic utensils, having closed the doors and windows, and having taken leave of the dwelling, should depart.
If there is no monk present, a novice should be asked for leave.”
If there is no novice monk, a monastery attendant should be asked for permission.
If there is no monastery attendant, a lay follower should be asked for permission.
If there is neither a monk, nor a novice, nor a monastery attendant, nor a lay follower, [one should place] a bed on four stones.
Having arranged bed upon bed and bench upon bench, having stacked the lodgings on top,
having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, and having closed the doors and windows,
one should depart. If the dwelling is leaking, if one is able, it should be roofed over, or an effort should be made to do so.
‘How indeed might this dwelling be roofed over?
If it could be obtained thus, that would be good.
If it could not be obtained, then in a place sheltered from the rain, having prepared a couch upon four stones—
Having moved bed from bed and stool from stool, having stacked the lodgings on top,
having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, and having closed the doors and windows, one should depart.
If the entire monastery is leaking, if one is able, the lodgings should be carried to the village, or an effort should be made to do so.
‘How indeed might this lodging be carried to the village?
If it can be done thus, that is good.
If it cannot be done, having prepared a bed upon four stones in the open air and having placed one bed upon another, [one should lie down].
Having moved the bed from its seat to another bed, having piled up the bedding on top, and having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils,
one should depart after covering them with grass or leaves,
thinking: "Perhaps even some parts might remain."
“Monks, this is the proper conduct for monks who are traveling, in accordance with which traveling monks should behave correctly.
Now at that time, the monks did not offer an expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*) in the dining hall.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, fail to offer words of thanksgiving at the head of the meal?
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to offer an expression of appreciation in the dining hall.”
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus, "By whom,
indeed, should the expression of thanksgiving be made at the meal?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow, bhikkhus, for a senior bhikkhu to give the expression of thanksgiving (anumodanā) in the meal hall.
Now at that time, a certain group had provided a meal for the Saṅgha.
The Venerable Sāriputta was the senior elder of the Saṅgha.
The monks thought,
"It has been permitted by the Blessed One that a senior monk may offer the expression of thanksgiving in the dining hall."
They departed, leaving the Venerable Sāriputta all alone.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having exchanged greetings with those people, proceeded on alone behind them.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Sāriputta coming from afar, all by himself.
Having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“I hope, Sāriputta, that the meal was successful?
“The meal was indeed successful, Bhante.”
"Moreover, the monks have departed, leaving me all alone.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the monks:
"Monks, I allow four or five senior or junior monks to wait for you in the dining hall."
Now at that time, a certain elder, having been called into the dining hall, waited for his turn.
Being unable to hold back his excrement, he fainted and fell down.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, when there is business to be done, to go after having asked permission from the monk who is next in seniority.
5. Discussion on the Duties Regarding the Refectory Now at that time, the group of six monks were poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum.
They go to the head of the meal hall; they even bypass the senior monks and walk right in front of them;
they sit down intruding upon the senior monks; they preempt the seats for the junior monks; and they sit in inhabited dwellings with their outer robes spread out.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six bhikkhus go to the dining hall poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum;
how can they even bypass the elder bhikkhus and walk right in front of them, and likewise the elders?”
“Those monks will sit down intruding upon us; they will even preempt new monks from seats;
and they will sit in inhabited areas having spread out their outer robes.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks go to the dining hall poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum;
that they even bypass and walk right in front of the elder monks;
that they sit down intruding upon the elder monks; that they block the new monks from their seats; and that they even spread out their outer robes [over the seats]?”
“Is it true, Blessed One, that she was sitting in a house between [buildings]?
“It is true, Blessed One. … Having rebuked her … pe … [the Buddha spoke].
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, I shall lay down the duties for the meal hall, according to which the bhikkhus must conduct themselves properly in the meal hall.
If it has been announced that it is time in the monastery, one should put on the lower robe all around, covering the three circles, and fasten the waistband.”
Having fastened the waistband, having put on the outer robes, having adjusted the neck-tie, and having washed and taken up the bowl,
one should enter the village carefully and without haste.
One must not go ahead, bypassing the elder bhikkhus.
One should walk with well-covered body in inhabited areas;
one should walk with well-restrained senses in inhabited areas;
one should walk with downcast eyes in inhabited areas.
One should not walk through a village with the body lifted up.
One should not walk through a village laughing loudly.
One should walk through a village with little sound.
One should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the body;
one should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the arms;
one should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the head.
One should not walk between houses with hands on the hips.
One should not walk between houses with the head covered.
One should not walk between houses in a crouching posture.
One should sit well-covered within a house.
One should sit well-restrained within a house.
One should sit with downcast eyes within a house.
One should not sit with one's body raised up in an inhabited area;
one should not sit laughing loudly in an inhabited area;
one should sit with little noise in an inhabited area.
One should not sit in an inhabited area swaying the body;
one should not sit in an inhabited area swaying the arms;
one should not sit in an inhabited area swaying the head.
One should not sit in an inhabited area with hands on the hips.
One should not sit in an inhabited area with the head covered.
One should not sit in an inhabited area with arms crossed over the chest.
One should not sit intruding upon senior bhikkhus.
One should not preempt new bhikkhus from their seats.
One should not sit in an inhabited area with one’s outer robe spread out.
When water is being given, one should receive the water by holding the bowl with both hands.
Having lowered it, the bowl should be washed carefully without scraping it.
If there is someone to receive the water, one should pour the water into the water-receiver after having lowered the bowl.
"Let the water-receiver not sprinkle with water; let the surrounding monks not sprinkle with water; let the outer robe not be sprinkled with water.
If there is no water-receiver, one should pour the water on the ground after lowering [the bowl], thinking:
"Let the surrounding monks not be sprinkled with water; let the outer robe not be sprinkled with water."
When rice is being given, one should receive the rice by taking the bowl with both hands, leaving space for the soup.
If there is ghee, oil, or additional curry, the senior monk should say:
“Distribute it equally among everyone.”
Almsfood should be received with care.
Almsfood should be received with mindfulness of the bowl.
Almsfood should be received with equal portions of curry.
Almsfood should be accepted when it is level with the rim of the bowl.
The elder should not eat until the rice has been served to everyone.
Almsfood should be eaten with careful attention.
Almsfood should be eaten perceiving it as a bowl.
Almsfood should be eaten in successive order.
Almsfood should be eaten with an equal amount of curry.
Almsfood should not be eaten by pressing it down into a heap.
One should not cover curry or sauce with rice out of a desire for more.
One who is not ill should not cause curry or rice to be requested for one's own sake and then eat it.
One should not look at the bowl of others with a mind of reproach.
One should not make a mouthful too large.
One should make the mouthful round.
One should not open the mouth until a morsel has been brought to it.
One should not thrust the entire hand into the mouth while eating.
One should not speak with a morsel in the mouth.
One should not eat by tossing morsels into the mouth; one should not eat by breaking off pieces of the ball of food;
one should not eat stuffing the cheeks.
One should not eat shaking the hand;
one should not eat scattering rice grains;
one should not eat sticking out the tongue.
One should not eat making a "capucapu" sound;
one should not eat making a "surusuru" sound;
one should not eat licking the hands.
One should not eat licking the bowl.
One should not eat licking the lips.
One should not receive a water vessel with a hand that has food on it.
The elder should not accept water until everyone has finished eating.
When water is being given, he should accept the water after receiving the bowl with both hands.
He should wash the bowl carefully, holding it low and without scraping it against anything.
If there is someone to receive the water, one should pour the water into the water-receptacle while keeping it low, thinking:
"May the person receiving the water not be splashed by the water; may the monks nearby not be splashed by the water; may the outer robe not be splashed by the water.
If there is no one to receive the water, one should pour the water on the ground while keeping it low.
"Let the neighboring monks not sprinkle water [on the path]; let the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) not be sprinkled with water.
One must not discard bowl-washing water containing rice grains within an inhabited area.
When returning, the junior monks should return first, and the elders afterwards.
One should walk with well-covered body in inhabited areas;
one should walk with well-restrained senses in inhabited areas;
one should walk with downcast eyes in inhabited areas.
One should not walk through an inhabited area with the body lifted up.
One should not walk through an inhabited area laughing loudly.
One should walk through an inhabited area with little noise.
One should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the body;
one should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the arms;
one should not walk through inhabited areas swaying the head.
One should not walk between houses leaning on a staff.
One should not walk between houses with one’s head covered.
One should not walk between houses in a squatting posture.
"This, monks, is the duty regarding the meal hall for monks, according to which monks should conduct themselves properly in the meal hall.
The first recitation section is finished.
6. Discussion on the Duties of One Who Goes for Alms.
Now at that time, monks going for alms were poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum as they wandered for alms;
they entered dwellings without observation and left them without observation;
they entered too hastily and left too hastily; they stood too far away and [too close].
They stood there; they stood for a very long time; they turned back even after a great while.
A certain monk who was wandering for alms, failing to observe his surroundings, entered a residence.
Thinking it was the door, he entered a certain inner room.
In that room as well, a woman was lying naked on her back.
That bhikkhu saw the woman lying naked on her back;
having seen her—
“This is not the door; this is a small room,” she said, and she emerged from that room.
Her husband saw that woman lying there naked on her back.
Having seen her, he—
“This monk has defiled my wife,” he said, and seizing that monk, he beat him.
Then that woman, waking up at the sound of it, said this to the man:
“Noble sir, why are you beating this monk?”
“Have you been defiled by this monk?
“No, noble lady, I have not been defiled by this monk;
that monk is innocent,” she said, and had the monk released.
Then that bhikkhu went to the monastery and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged it, and complained, saying:
"How can these alms-collecting bhikkhus, poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum, go for alms?"
“They will walk about; they will enter the dwelling without observing it; they will exit without observing it;
they will enter too hastily; they will exit too hastily; they will stand too far away;
they will stand too close; they will stay for too long; and they will turn back too quickly.”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that such a thing has occurred?"...
"It is true, Blessed One," they replied... [as before].
Having rebuked them...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Therefore, bhikkhus, I shall lay down the proper conduct for bhikkhus who go for alms, so that bhikkhus who go for alms may conduct themselves correctly.”
“Monks, a monk who goes for alms, thinking,
‘Now I shall enter the village,’ should cover the three circles, put on his lower robe properly,
fasten his waistband, button up his outer robes, tie the toggle, and wash his bowl.”
Having taken [the bowl], one should enter the village with care and without haste.
One should walk within the village well-covered;
one should walk within the village well-restrained.
One should walk with downcast eyes within an inhabited area.
One should not walk with the body tossed about within an inhabited area.
One should not walk laughing loudly within an inhabited area.
One should walk with little sound within an inhabited area.
One should not walk swaying the body within an inhabited area.
One should not walk swinging the arms within an inhabited area.
One should not walk among the houses shaking one’s head.
One should not walk among the houses with hands on the hips.
One should not walk among the houses with the head covered.
One should not walk on one's heels within an inhabited area.
When entering a dwelling, one should observe:
"By this way I shall enter; by this way I shall exit."
One should not enter too hastily.
One should not depart too hastily.
One should not stand too far away.
One should not stand too close;
one should not stand for too long;
one should not turn back too quickly.
He should observe with a steady gaze:
“Does she wish to give alms, or does she not wish to give?
If she sets aside her work, or rises from her seat, or touches the spoon, or touches the bowl, or puts it down, he should conclude: “She wishes to give.”
When alms are being given, one should lift up the outer robe with the left hand, incline the bowl with the right hand, and receive the alms by taking hold of the bowl with both hands.
One must not look at the face of the person giving the alms.
One should observe:
‘Whether she wishes to give soup or does not wish to give it.
If she touches the spoon, or touches the vessel, or sets it down—
it should be understood that she wishes to give it.
When alms have been given, one should cover the bowl with the outer robe and turn back carefully and without haste.
One should walk through inhabited areas well-covered;
one should walk through inhabited areas well-restrained.
One should walk with downcast eyes within an inhabited area.
One should not walk with the body held high within an inhabited area.
One should not walk laughing loudly within an inhabited area.
One should walk with little noise in inhabited areas.
One should not walk swaying the body in inhabited areas.
One should not walk swaying the arms in inhabited areas.
One should not walk in an inhabited area shaking one’s head;
one should not walk in an inhabited area with hands on the hips;
one should not walk in an inhabited area with the head covered.
One should not walk on tiptoe within an inhabited area.
Whoever returns first from the village for alms should prepare a seat, set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone;
having washed the bowl for refuse, it should be set aside, and drinking water and water for rinsing should be provided.
When one returns from the village for alms, if there is food remaining from what was eaten and if he so desires, it may be eaten.
If he does not desire it, it should be discarded in a place with little vegetation, or thrown into water where there are no living beings.
He should then lift up the seat, put away the foot-water, the footstool, the foot-washing stone, and the bowl for scraps.
Having washed [the vessels], they should be put away; the drinking water and the water for washing should be put away; the dining hall should be swept.
Whoever sees that the drinking-water jar, the water-for-washing jar, or the toilet-water jar is empty or void should fill it.
If it is too heavy for him to lift, he should call a second person by a gesture of the hand and fill it by passing it from hand to hand; on that account, he must not break into speech.
“Monks, this is the duty for monks who go on almsround, the way in which monks who go on almsround should conduct themselves properly.
Now at that time, a number of monks were dwelling in the forest.

They did not provide drinking water, nor did they provide water for washing; they did not maintain a fire, nor did they maintain a set of kindling sticks; they did not know the lunar mansions, nor did they know the directions.
When thieves went there, they said to those bhikkhus, "Venerable sirs, is there drinking water?"
“There is none, friends.
“Is there any water for rinsing, venerable sir?
“There is none, friends.”
“Is there, venerable sir, a fire?”— “There is not,
friend.”— “Is there,
venerable sir, a fire-stick apparatus?”— “There is.”
“There is none, friend.
(…) “With what, venerable sir, are you occupied today?
“We do not know, friend.”
“Venerable sir, which direction is this?
“We do not know, friend,” they replied.
Then those thieves—
“There is no drinking water here, no water for washing, no fire, and no fire-drills. They do not know the constellations, nor do they know the directions.
These are thieves; these are not monks.
Having struck them [with their sticks], they departed.
Then those monks reported this matter to other monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, I will prescribe the proper conduct for forest-dwelling monks, as it is by forest-dwelling monks that one should properly conduct oneself.
A forest-dwelling monk, monks, having risen early, should put his bowl into its bag, hang it over his shoulder,
place his robe on his back, put on his sandals, and put away his wooden and earthenware utensils.”
Having closed the doors and windows, one should descend from the lodging,
thinking, "Now I shall enter the village. Having removed the sandals,
placed them low, dusted them off, put them into the bag, and slung the bag over the shoulder, [one should perform] the threefold [circumambulation].

One who is entering [a village] should put on the lower robe evenly all around, fasten the waistband, arrange the upper robes with their folds tucked in, put on the outer cloak, fasten the toggle, wash the bowl, take it up, and enter the village carefully and without haste.
One should walk within inhabited areas well-covered... [and so forth].
One should not walk among the houses with hands on the hips.
One should not walk among the houses with the head covered.
One should not walk among the houses squatting.
One entering a dwelling should observe:
"By this way I shall enter; by this way I shall exit.
One should not enter with excessive haste.
One should not depart too hastily.
One should not stand too far away.
One should not stand too close.
One should not stand for too long;
one should not turn back too quickly.
While standing, one should observe:
‘Whether she wishes to give alms or does not wish to give alms.
If she sets aside her work, or rises from her seat, or touches the spoon, or touches the vessel, or puts it down—
it should be understood that she wishes to give.

When alms are being given, one should lift up the outer robe with the left hand, incline the bowl with the right hand, receive the alms by taking hold of the bowl with both hands, and accept the alms.
One must not look at the face of the giver of the alms.
One should observe:
‘Whether she wishes to give soup or does not wish to give it.
If she touches the spoon, or touches the bowl, or sets it down—
it should be understood that she wishes to give it.
When alms have been given, one should cover the bowl with the outer robe and turn back carefully and without haste.
One should walk through inhabited areas well-covered [with robes]...
[and so on] ...one should not walk through inhabited areas in a squatting posture.

Having departed from the village, the bowl should be placed in its bag, slung over the shoulder, the robe should be folded and placed on the head, sandals should be put on, and then one should go. Monks,
a forest-dwelling monk should provide drinking water, he should provide water for washing, he should maintain a fire,
he should maintain a set of kindling sticks, he should maintain a walking stick, and he should learn the constellations.
Whether in their entirety or in part, one must be skilled regarding the directions.
This, monks, is the duty for forest-dwelling bhikkhus, according to which forest-dwelling bhikkhus should conduct themselves properly.
8. Discussion on the Duty Concerning Lodgings.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were doing robe-work in the open air.
The group-of-six bhikkhus shook out their lodgings in a courtyard against the wind;
the bhikkhus were covered with dust.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks shake down their lodgings in an open courtyard against the wind?
They have covered the monks with dust!"

Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group-of-six bhikkhus shake out their lodgings in the open courtyard against the wind, thereby scattering dust over the other bhikkhus?
“It is true, Blessed One. … [as before] …
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, I shall lay down the proper conduct regarding lodgings for the monks, according to which the monks must behave properly toward lodgings.”
In whatever dwelling he dwells, if that dwelling is dirty, it should be cleaned if he is able to do so.
When cleaning the dwelling, first the bowl and robe should be taken out and placed to one side;
the sitting mat and the rug should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or let it brush against the surface of the door.
Having lowered the bench, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or let it brush against the surface of the door.
The bed-legs should be removed and placed to one side;
the spittoon should be removed and placed to one side;
the leaning-board should be removed and placed to one side.
Having inspected the floor-covering as it was laid out, one should remove it and set it aside to one side.
If there is a cobweb in the dwelling, it should first be removed from the ceiling; the light-fittings, corners, and edges should be wiped clean.
If the wall has been treated with red ocher and is moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be wiped clean with a cloth that has been soaked and wrung out.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled repeatedly with water and then swept, thinking:
"Lest the monastery be covered with dust."
Having sifted through the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
One should not shake bedding near the vicinity of monks,
nor should one shake bedding near the vicinity of the monastery.
One should not shake out bedding near drinking water.
One should not shake out bedding near water for washing.
One should not shake out bedding in an open courtyard where it is against the wind.
In the downwind direction, the bedding should be beaten.
Having dried the floor-covering to one side, cleaned it, beaten it, and brought it back, it should be spread out as it was originally arranged.
Having dried the bed-legs to one side, wiped them, and brought them back, they should be placed in their proper positions.

Having taken the bed to one side, dried it, cleaned it, and beaten the dust from it, and having lowered it, he should bring it back and arrange it as prescribed, doing so carefully without scraping it or knocking it against the surface of the door.

Having taken the chair to one side, dried it, cleaned it, and beaten the dust from it, and having lowered it, he should bring it back and arrange it as prescribed, doing so carefully without scraping it or knocking it against the surface of the door.
Having dried the mattress and pillow cover on one side, having cleaned it, having beaten it, and having brought it back, it should be spread out as previously arranged.
Having dried the sitting mat and rug on one side, having cleaned them, having beaten them, and having brought them back, they should be spread out as previously arranged.
Having dried the spittoon on one side, having wiped it, and having brought it back, it should be placed in its proper place.
Having dried the wooden plank in one place, wiped it clean, and brought it back, it should be placed in its proper position.
The bowl and robe should be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and, touching the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the chair with the other hand, set the bowl down.
Furthermore, the robe must not be placed on ground that has not been cleared.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, arrange the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then place the robe away.
If dusty winds are blowing from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is the cold season, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night.
If it is the hot season, the windows should be closed by day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If washing water is not available, washing water should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water must be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
If one dwells in the same monastery as an elder, one should not give a recitation,
nor ask questions, nor engage in study, nor speak on the Dhamma, nor light a lamp without having asked the elder’s permission.
The lamp must not be extinguished; the windows must not be opened, nor must they be closed.
If he walks back and forth on the same walking path as an elder, he should turn toward where the elder is, and he must not brush against the elder with the corner of his outer robe.
This, monks, is the proper conduct regarding lodgings, according to which monks should behave properly toward the lodgings.”

9. The Discussion on the Conduct Regarding the Sauna Now at that time, the group of six monks, being restrained by the elder monks in the sauna, out of disrespect piled up a great quantity of wood, set it on fire, closed the door, and sat down at the doorway.
The other monks, overcome by the heat and unable to find the door, fainted and fell down.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can the group-of-six monks, when being restrained by the elder monks in the sauna, out of disrespect pile up a great deal of wood, set fire to it, close the door, and sit at the door?
The monks, overcome by heat and unable to get to the door, faint and fall down!"
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...

"Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group-of-six bhikkhus, when being restrained by elder bhikkhus in the sauna, out of disrespect piled up a great deal of wood, set fire to it, closed the door, and sat down at the door;
and that the bhikkhus, overcome by the heat and unable to find the door, fainted and fell?"
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, when a senior monk is being restrained in a sauna, he must not, out of disrespect, pile up a large amount of wood and set fire to it.
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, one must not sit at the door after having closed it.”
Whoever should sit down [there], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Therefore, monks, I shall lay down the proper conduct for the sauna (jantāghara-vatta) for the monks, according to which the monks must behave correctly in the sauna.
Whoever goes first to the sauna, if the ashes have accumulated, the ashes should be discarded.
If the sauna is dirty, the sauna should be swept.
If the surrounding area is dirty, the surrounding area should be swept.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse must be swept.
If the sauna hall is dirty, the sauna hall must be swept.
Powdered soap must be prepared, clay must be moistened, and water must be poured into the water trough.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks,
nor should one block the junior monks from their seats.
If he is able, he should perform services for the elder bhikkhus in the sauna.
When leaving the sauna, he should take the sauna-bench and depart from the sauna while shielding it both in front and behind.
If he is able, he should also perform services for the elder bhikkhus in the water.
One should not bathe in front of the elder bhikkhus, nor should one bathe upstream from them.
When emerging after bathing, one should yield the path to those who are entering.
Whoever leaves the sauna last should wash it if it is muddy.

“Having washed the clay trough, put away the sauna-bench, extinguished the fire, and closed the door, one should depart. This, monks, is the duty for the sauna regarding how monks should conduct themselves properly in the sauna.

10. Discussion on the Duty Concerning the Latrine [The Buddha said: “Monks, I will lay down the duties concerning the latrine. Listen and pay close attention; I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, a monk who intends to enter the latrine should first take a leaf, a blade of grass, or a piece of cloth and cover the ground. Having entered the latrine, he should not stand too long over the pot. He should not wipe himself with a brick, a stone, or a shard. He should not throw the used wiping material outside the latrine while standing on the threshold. He should not throw it onto the path, nor onto the waterway, nor onto a place where people walk. When a monk has finished using the latrine, he should take a leaf, a blade of grass, or a piece of cloth and cover the ground. Having entered the latrine, he should not stand too long over the pot. He should not wipe himself with a brick, a stone, or a shard. He should not throw the used wiping material outside the latrine while standing on the threshold. He should not throw it onto the path, nor onto the waterway, nor onto a place where people walk. A monk who intends to clean the latrine should first take a leaf, a blade of grass, or a piece of cloth and cover the ground. Having entered the latrine, he should not stand too long over the pot. He should not wipe himself with a brick, a stone, or a shard. He should not throw the used wiping material outside the latrine while standing on the threshold. He should not throw it onto the path, nor onto the waterway, nor onto a place where people walk. When a monk has finished cleaning the latrine, he should take a leaf, a blade of grass, or a piece of cloth and cover the ground. Having entered the latrine, he should not stand too long over the pot. He should not wipe himself with a brick, a stone, or a shard. He should not throw the used wiping material outside the latrine while standing on the threshold. He should not throw it onto the path, nor onto the waterway, nor onto a place where people walk. This, monks, is the duty concerning the latrine regarding how monks should conduct themselves properly in the latrine.”
Now at that time, a certain monk of brahmin birth, having defecated, did not wish to rinse himself, thinking,
"Who would touch this outcaste, this foul-smelling thing?
A worm settled in his anus.
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus:
"But why, friend, did you not rinse your mouth after defecating?
"It is so, friends."
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying, "How can a monk, having defecated, not rinse with water?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, bhikkhu, that you do not rinse your mouth after defecating?
“It is true, Blessed One. … Having rebuked him … [the Buddha spoke] …
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, having defecated, one should not fail to rinse with water when water is available.
Whoever should fail to rinse commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the monks were using the restroom according to their seniority.
The junior monks, having arrived first, would defecate and wait for others to come.
Holding back their excrement, they became faint and collapsed.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"Is it true, monks, that such a thing has occurred?"...
"It is true, Blessed One."... [as before] ...
“Monks, one should not defecate in the restroom according to seniority.
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to defecate according to the order of arrival.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks entered the restroom too hastily,
they entered even by jumping over the threshold, they defecated while snorting, they defecated while chewing tooth-sticks,
they defecated outside the toilet pit, and they urinated outside the urinal pit.
They spit into the urinal trough; they scrape with a rough stick; they throw even the scraping sticks into the cesspool;
they exit too hastily; they exit by jumping up; they rinse their mouths making a "capu-capu" sound;
and they leave water remaining in the rinsing bowls.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six bhikkhus enter the restroom with such haste,
enter it after lifting up the door-latch, defecate while snorting, and defecate while chewing tooth-sticks?”
They will defecate outside the latrine pit; they will urinate outside the urinal pit;
they will spit into the urinal pit; they will scrape with a rough stick; they will throw the scraping stick into the cesspool;
they will exit too hastily; and they will exit by jumping up.
“They will even gargle with a splashing sound, and water will remain left over in their rinsing bowls.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ... “Is it true, bhikkhus, that you do so?”...
[as before] ... “It is true, Bhagavā.”... [as before] ... “Bhikkhus, from today onward, I allow rinsing bowls.”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Therefore, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for monks regarding the restroom, so that the restroom may be used correctly by the monks.
Whoever goes to the restroom should cough while standing outside.
He should also cough while sitting inside.”
Having hung up the robe on a robe-stand or a robe-line, one should enter the restroom carefully and without haste.
One should not enter too forcefully,
nor should one enter with the robe tucked up.
One should void excrement while standing on a toilet-slat.
One should not void excrement while sneezing.
One should not void excrement while chewing a tooth-stick.
One should not void excrement outside on the excrement-ditch.
One should not urinate outside on the urine-ditch.
One should not spit on the urine-ditch.
One should not scrape with a rough stick.
One should not throw the scraping stick into the cesspool.
While standing on the toilet footstool, one should cover oneself.
One should not go out too hastily.
One should not go out by jumping up.
One should jump up while standing on the rinsing-sandals.
One should not rinse the mouth making a "capucapu" sound.
One should not leave water remaining in the rinsing bowl.
While standing on the rinsing footstool, one should cover [the body].
If the restroom has been fouled, it should be washed.
If the receptacle for wiping sticks is full, the wiping sticks should be discarded.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If the veranda is dirty, the veranda should be swept.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
“If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water must be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
This, monks, is the duty regarding the restroom for monks, according to which monks should properly conduct themselves in the restroom.
11. Discussion on the Duties Toward a Preceptor (Upajjhāyavattakathā)
Now at that time, the co-residents were not conducting themselves properly toward their preceptors.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these co-residents not conduct themselves properly toward their preceptors?"
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus,
that the students are not conducting themselves properly toward their preceptors?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can it be, monks, that students do not conduct themselves properly toward their preceptors?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
Having rebuked them … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, I shall lay down the proper conduct for co-resident pupils toward their preceptors, as it should be rightly observed by co-resident pupils toward their preceptors.”
“Monks, a co-resident disciple should conduct himself properly toward his preceptor.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
having risen early, removing his sandals, and arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, he should offer a tooth-stick and water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.”
If there is rice gruel, having washed the vessel, the gruel should be offered.
After he has drunk the gruel, water should be given to him; then, taking back the vessel, holding it low and washing it carefully without clashing it against anything, it should be put away.
When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be removed.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.

If the preceptor wishes to enter the village, the inner robe should be given to him; the outer robe should be received back; the waistband should be given; the upper robes should be given after being folded and rolled up; and the bowl, having been washed and rinsed with water, should be given.
If the preceptor desires an attendant monk, [the attendant] should dress himself properly, covering the three circles and wearing the lower robe evenly.

Having fastened his waistband, having put on his upper robe, having donned the outer robes, having tied the neck-fastener, and having washed and taken his bowl, he should act as the attendant monk behind his preceptor.
He should not walk too far behind nor too close; he should receive whatever is placed into the bowl.
One should not interrupt the preceptor with side remarks while he is speaking.
If the preceptor speaks concerning an offense, he should be stopped.
When returning, one should arrive first and prepare a seat, as well as water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scraper.
He should set out a seat; he should go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robe; he should give him an inner robe and receive his lower robe.
If the robe is damp, it should be dried for a short while in the sun, but the robe must not be left in the sun.
The robe should be folded.
When folding the robe, one should fold it with a four-finger-width border turned up so that there is no tearing in the middle.
The waistband should be put on.
If there is almsfood and the preceptor wishes to eat, the almsfood should be offered after giving water.
The preceptor should be asked for drinking water.

Having given water to the one who has finished eating, and having received the bowl, he should hold it low and wash it carefully without scratching it; then, having removed the water, it should be dried for a short while in the warmth.
However, the bowl must not be placed directly in the heat.
The bowl and robe should then be set aside.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, touch the base of the bed or the base of the chair with the other hand, and then put away the bowl.
The bowl must not be put away on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the outside and the fold toward the inside, and then put away the robe.
When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be removed; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper should be put away.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the preceptor wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared;
if there is need for heat, heat should be prepared.
If the preceptor wishes to enter the sauna, powder should be kneaded and clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should follow closely behind his preceptor;
having offered the sauna-bench and received the robe, he should set it aside to one side. He should provide the powder and the clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks,
nor should one block the junior monks from their seats.
Service should be rendered to the preceptor in the sauna.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover it both in front and behind, and then exit the sauna.
Service should also be rendered to the preceptor in the water.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried his limbs, and put on his lower robe,
he should wipe the water from his preceptor’s body, give him his lower robe, and give him his upper robe. Taking the sauna bench,
he should return first, prepare a seat, and set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot scraper.
The preceptor should be asked for water.
If he wishes to give an instruction, he should be instructed.
If he wishes to ask questions, he should be questioned.
In whatever monastery the preceptor resides, if that monastery is dirty and he is able to do so, it should be cleaned.
When cleaning the monastery, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side;
the sitting mat and the rug should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the door frame.
Having lowered the bench, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the door frame.
The bed-legs should be removed and placed to one side;
the spittoon should be removed and placed to one side;
the leaning-board should be removed and placed to one side.
Having inspected the floor-covering as it was laid out and removed it, it should be placed aside.
If there is a crack in the dwelling, the ceiling first must be lowered; the light-shafts, corners, and edges must be wiped clean.
If a wall treated with red ocher has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be wiped clean after moistening and pressing down a cloth.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled with water again and again and then swept, thinking:
"Lest the monastery be covered in dust."
Having sifted through the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having aired, cleaned, and beaten out the ground-covering, it should be brought back and spread out as it was previously arranged.
Having aired and wiped the bed-legs, they should be brought back and placed in their proper positions.

Having dried the bed in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, and lowered it, one should bring it back and arrange it as previously set out, doing so carefully without scratching it or knocking it against the surface of the door.

Having dried the chair in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, and lowered it, one should bring it back and arrange it as previously set out, doing so carefully without scratching it or knocking it against the surface of the door.
Having dried the mattress and pillow in the sun, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should bring them back and arrange them as previously set out.
The sitting mat and the rug should be dried in the sun, cleaned, beaten to remove dust, brought back inside, and spread out as they were previously arranged.
The spittoon should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The leaning board should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes must be set aside.
When setting aside the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the base of the bed or the base of the seat, and then set the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe-cloth, one should take hold of the cloth with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward oneself and the body toward the outside, and then put it away.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night.
If it is hot weather, the windows should be closed during the day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If water for washing is not available, water for washing should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing pitcher, the rinsing pitcher should be filled with water.

If dissatisfaction arises in the preceptor, the student living with him should dispel it, have it dispelled, or give a Dhamma talk to him. If remorse arises in the preceptor, the student living with him should remove it, have it removed, or give a Dhamma talk to him.
If a wrong view arises in the preceptor, the student living with him should disentangle him from it, have him disentangled from it, or give a Dhamma talk to him.
If the preceptor has committed a grave offense and is subject to probation, the student living with him should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha grant probation to my preceptor?
If the preceptor is subject to being sent back to the beginning, the student living with him should make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha send the preceptor back to the beginning?
If the preceptor is deserving of the trial period (*mānatta*), the student living with him (*saddhivihārika*) should make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the trial period to the preceptor?"
If the preceptor is deserving of rehabilitation, the student living with him should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Sangha rehabilitate the preceptor?

If the Sangha intends to perform a formal act against the preceptor—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the student living with him should make an effort.
"How might the Saṅgha not perform a formal act against my preceptor, or how might it transform a heavy one into a light one?

Or, if a formal act has already been performed against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the student living with him should make an effort:
"How might my preceptor conduct himself properly, behave in accordance with the hair-raising [Dharma], and live in such a way that the Saṅgha would rescind that formal act?"
If the preceptor’s robe needs washing, it should be washed by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
“How can my preceptor’s robe be washed?
If the preceptor’s robe needs making, it should be made by the student, or he should make an effort.
"How indeed should the preceptor’s robe be prepared?
If the dye for the preceptor needs to be boiled, it should be boiled by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How indeed can the dye for the preceptor be boiled?"
If the preceptor’s robe needs dyeing, the student should dye it himself or make an effort to have it dyed, thinking, “How can my preceptor’s robe be dyed?
When dyeing the robe, he should turn it over carefully again and again while dyeing; he must not leave while the drops of dye are still dripping.
Without having asked one's preceptor, one must not give an almsbowl to anyone, nor receive an almsbowl from anyone;
one must not give a robe to anyone, nor receive a robe from anyone;
one must not give requisites to anyone, nor receive requisites from anyone.
One should not have one person’s hair cut, nor should one have another person’s hair cut;
one should not perform service for one person, nor should one have service performed by another;
one should not do a favor for one person, nor should one have a favor done for another.
One should not act as a junior attendant for anyone else, nor should anyone be taken as a junior attendant by oneself;
one should not have almsfood brought out for anyone else, nor should one have almsfood brought out by oneself;
one should not enter a village without having asked permission from one’s preceptor.
One should not go to a cemetery;
one should not depart for distant regions.
If one’s preceptor is ill, one should attend to him for as long as life lasts, and one should wait for his recovery.
“This, monks, is the duty toward preceptors for those living with them as pupils; this is how pupils should properly conduct themselves toward their preceptors.
Now at that time, preceptors were not conducting themselves properly toward their pupils.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires… [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can preceptors not conduct themselves properly toward their students?
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One… [as before].
“Is it true, monks, that preceptors do not behave properly toward their co-residents?
“It is true, Blessed One. … Having rebuked them … [the Buddha spoke as follows] …
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, I will lay down the proper conduct for preceptors toward their co-residents, so that preceptors may behave correctly toward their co-residents.
Bhikkhus, a preceptor must behave properly toward his co-resident.”
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
Monks, a student should be supported and assisted by his preceptor through recitation, interrogation, exhortation, and instruction.
If the preceptor has an alms bowl but the student does not have one, the preceptor should give the bowl to the student, or he should make an effort to obtain one for him.
"How might an almsbowl arise for my student?
If the preceptor has a robe but the student has no robe, the preceptor should give a robe to the student, or he should make an effort, thinking: "How might a robe arise for my student?"
If the preceptor has requisites and the student has none, the preceptor must give the requisites to the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How can requisites be obtained for the student?
If the student is ill, having risen early, the preceptor should give him a tooth-stick, water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is rice gruel, he should wash the vessel and offer the gruel.
When the student has drunk the gruel, he should give him water, receive the vessel, hold it low, and wash it carefully without clashing it against anything, then set it aside.
Once the student has risen, the seat should be put away.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.
If the student (saddhivihārika) wishes to enter the village, the lower robe should be given to him,
the upper robe received back, the waistband should be given, the outer robes should be given after being folded together, and the bowl should be given washed and with water for rinsing.
Thinking, "He will turn back at this point," one should prepare a seat; water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone should be set out;
having gone forth to meet him, his bowl and robe should be received; an inner garment should be given, and his lower robe should be received.
If a robe is damp, it should be dried in the sun for a short while, but the robe must not be left in the sun.
The robe should be folded.
When folding the robe, one should fold it after turning back the edges by four finger-widths.
"Lest there be a breakage in the middle," he said.
"The waist-band should be fastened around the body.
If there is almsfood and the student wishes to eat, one should give him water and offer the almsfood."
The co-resident student should be asked whether he has had enough water to drink.

After the teacher has finished eating, the student should give him water, receive the bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it, and let it warm for a short while in the heat; however, the bowl must not be left out in the heat.
The bowl and robes should then be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, touch the area beneath the bed or beneath the bench with the other hand, and then set down the bowl.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.
