When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-rack or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the outer side and the fold toward the inner side, and then put away the robe.
When the student has risen, the seat should be put away; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper should be set aside.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the student wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared.
If there is need for heat, heat should be prepared.
If the student living with him wishes to enter the sauna, powder should be kneaded and clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should go and give the sauna-bench [to the resident], receive the robe, and set it aside to one side.
He should provide powder and clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna.
When entering a sauna, one should smear the face with clay and cover both the front and the back before entering.
One should not sit encroaching upon senior monks, nor should one block junior monks from their seats.
In the sauna, one should perform services for one’s co-resident pupil.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover oneself both in front and behind, and then depart from the sauna.
One should also perform services for the student in the water.
Having bathed, one should emerge first, dry one's own limbs, put on one's undergarment, and [assist] the student.
He should wipe the water from [the teacher’s] body, give him a lower robe, and give him an upper robe.
Taking a seat for the sauna, he should arrive first and prepare a seat. He should set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot scraper.
He should ask his co-resident pupil if he wants drinking water.
In whatever dwelling the student lives, if that dwelling is dirty and he is able to do so, it should be cleaned.
While cleaning the dwelling, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and set aside to one side...
[and so forth] ...if there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water should be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.

If dissatisfaction arises in the student, the preceptor should dispel it, have it dispelled, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him. If remorse arises in the student, the preceptor should remove it, have it removed, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
If a wrong view arises in the student, the preceptor should disentangle him from it, have him disentangled from it, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
If a co-resident student has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation, the preceptor must make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha grant probation to this co-resident student?
If a co-resident student is subject to being sent back to the beginning, the preceptor must make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha send the student back to the beginning?
If the student is deserving of the *mānatta* penance, the preceptor should make an effort:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to the student?"
If the student living with him is deserving of rehabilitation, the preceptor should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Sangha rehabilitate the student living with me?

If the Sangha intends to perform a formal act against the student living with him—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the preceptor should make an effort.
"How might the Saṅgha not carry out a formal act against the student, or how might it reduce it to a lighter one?

Or, if a formal act has already been carried out against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the preceptor should make an effort, thinking:
"How might the student conduct himself properly, act in accordance with the rules, and behave so as to deserve release, such that the Saṅgha might rescind that formal act?"
If the robe-cloth of a student needs washing, the preceptor should instruct him,
"Wash it in this way," or he should make an effort, thinking, "How can the student's robe-cloth be washed?
If the robe-cloth of a student needs making, the preceptor should instruct him, "Make it in this way."
Or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can I ensure that my student's robe is made?
If the student's dye needs to be boiled, the preceptor should instruct him:
"Boil it in this way," or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can I ensure that my student's dye is boiled?"
If the robe-cloth of a student is to be dyed, the preceptor should instruct him, “You should dye it like this,” or he should make an effort, thinking, “How can the student’s robe-cloth be dyed?
When dyeing the robe-cloth, it should be carefully turned over repeatedly; one must not depart while the drops of dye have not yet dried.
“If a co-resident student is ill, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts; his recovery must be awaited.
This, monks, is the duty toward co-resident students that preceptors should properly fulfill toward their co-resident students.
The second recitation section is finished.
13. Discussion on the Duties Toward Teachers.
Now at that time, pupils did not behave properly toward their teachers.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How indeed can disciples not behave properly toward their teachers?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that disciples do not behave properly toward their teachers?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
Having rebuked them and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for pupils toward their teachers, so that pupils may conduct themselves rightly toward their teachers.
Monks, a pupil must conduct himself rightly toward his teacher.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:”
Rising early, having removed his sandals, and having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, he should provide a tooth-stick and water for rinsing the mouth; he should prepare a seat.
If there is rice porridge, he should wash the vessel and bring the porridge forward.
When the teacher has drunk the porridge, he should give him water, receive the vessel, lower it, and wash it carefully without scratching it, then put it away.
When the teacher has risen, the seat should be removed.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.

If the teacher wishes to enter the village, the lower robe should be given to him, the upper robe received back from him, the waistband should be given, the outer robes should be given to him after being folded together, and the bowl should be washed and given to him with water.
If the teacher desires an attendant monk, one should cover the three circles,
put on the lower robe properly, fasten the waistband, put on the upper robes with the inner lining tucked in,
fasten the neck-loop, wash the bowl, take it up, and act as the teacher’s attendant monk.
One should not go too far away, nor should one go too close; one should receive the alms-food contained in the bowl.
One should not interrupt the teacher’s speech with talk in between.
If the teacher speaks concerning an offense, he should be stopped.
Returning first, one should prepare a seat; set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone;
go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robe; give him a spare lower garment and receive his own lower garment in return.
If a robe is damp, it should be dried in the warmth for a short while, but the robe must not be placed directly in the heat.
The robe should be folded.
When folding the robe, one should fold it after turning up the edge by four finger-breadths.
"Lest there be a break in the middle," he said.
"The waist-band should be fastened around the body.
If there is almsfood and the teacher wishes to eat, one should give water and then offer the almsfood."
The teacher should be asked for water.

After giving water to one who has finished eating, he should take the bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it, and let it dry for a short while in the warmth; however, the bowl should not be left in the heat.
The bowl and robes should then be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, touch the bottom of the bed or the bottom of the chair with the other hand, and then set down the bowl.
The bowl must not be set down on the ground unless it has been cleared of any intervening objects.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the outer side and the fold toward the inner side, and then put away the robe.
When the teacher has risen, the seat should be put away; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-washing slab should be set aside.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the teacher wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared;
if there is need for warmth, warmth should be prepared.
If the teacher wishes to enter the sauna, powder should be kneaded and clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should follow closely behind his teacher;
having offered the sauna-bench and received the robe, he should set it aside to one side. He should provide the bath-powder and the clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover both the front and the back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon senior bhikkhus,
nor should one block junior bhikkhus from their seats.
In the sauna, service should be performed for the teacher.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover it both in front and behind, and then exit the sauna.
In the water as well, service should be performed for the teacher.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried his limbs, and dressed himself,
he should wipe the water from the teacher’s body, give him his lower robe, and give him his upper robe. Taking the sauna-bench,
he should return first, prepare a seat, and set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scraper.
The teacher should be asked for water.
If he wishes to recite [the scriptures], he should be made to recite.
If he wishes to question [on the meaning], he should be questioned.
In whatever monastery the teacher resides, if that monastery is dirty, it should be cleaned if one has the energy to do so.
When cleaning the monastery, first the bowl and robe should be taken out and placed to one side;
the sitting mat and the sheet should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed and carefully carrying it out without striking or knocking it against the door frame, it should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bench and carefully carrying it out without striking or knocking it against the door frame, it should be placed to one side.
The bed-legs should be removed and placed to one side;
the spittoon should be removed and placed to one side;
the leaning-board should be removed and placed to one side.
Having observed the floor-covering as it was laid out, one should take it away and set it aside to one side.
If there are cobwebs in the dwelling, they should first be removed from the ceiling; the openings for light and the corners should be wiped clean.
If the wall treated with red ocher has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be wiped clean with a cloth that has been soaked and wrung out.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled repeatedly with water and then swept, thinking:
"Lest the monastery be covered in dust."
Having sifted through the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having aired, cleaned, and beaten out the floor-covering, and having brought it back inside, it should be spread out as it was previously arranged.
Having aired and wiped the bed-legs, and having brought them back inside, they should be placed in their proper positions.

Having dried the bed in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, and lowered it, one should bring it back and arrange it as prescribed, taking great care not to strike it or let it brush against the surface of the door.

Having dried the stool in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, and lowered it, one should bring it back and arrange it as prescribed, taking great care not to strike it or let it brush against the surface of the door.
Having dried the mattress and pillow in the sun, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should bring them back and arrange them as prescribed.
The sitting mat and spread should be dried, cleaned, beaten, brought back, and spread out as it was previously arranged.
The spittoon should be dried, wiped clean, brought back, and placed in its proper place.
The leaning-board should be dried, wiped clean, brought back, and placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes must be set aside.
When setting aside the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and, touching the area beneath the bed or the area beneath the seat with the other hand, set the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe-cloths, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then put the robe away.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night.
If it is hot, the windows should be closed during the day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If washing water is not available, washing water should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing pitcher, the rinsing pitcher should be filled with water.

If dissatisfaction arises in the teacher, the pupil should dispel it, have it dispelled, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him. If remorse arises in the teacher, the pupil should remove it, have it removed, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
If a wrong view arises in the teacher, the pupil should disentangle him from it, have him disentangled from it, or give a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
If the teacher has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation (parivāsa), the pupil must make an effort [to ensure] that the Saṅgha grants probation to the teacher, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant probation to my teacher?
If the teacher is subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), the pupil must make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha send the teacher back to the beginning?
If the teacher is deserving of the *mānatta* penance, the pupil must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to the teacher?"
If the teacher is deserving of rehabilitation, the pupil should make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Sangha rehabilitate the teacher?
If the Sangha intends to perform a formal act against the teacher—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the pupil should make an effort [to prevent it].
"How might the Saṅgha not perform a formal act against the teacher, or how might it transform a light one?
Furthermore, if a formal act has been performed against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the pupil must make an effort:
"How might the teacher behave properly, act in accordance with the rules, and conduct himself so as to reach the end of the matter, such that the Saṅgha might revoke that formal act?"
If the teacher’s robe needs washing, the pupil should wash it, or he should make an effort, thinking:
“How can the teacher’s robe be washed?
If the teacher’s robe needs making, the pupil should make it, or he should make an effort.
"How indeed should the teacher’s robe be prepared?
If the teacher’s dye needs to be boiled, the pupil should boil it, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How indeed can the teacher’s dye be boiled?"
If the teacher’s robe needs dyeing, the pupil should dye it himself or make an effort, thinking, “How can the teacher’s robe be dyed?
When dyeing the robe, he should dye it by turning it over carefully and repeatedly; he should not leave while the drops of dye have not yet dried.
Without having asked the teacher for permission, one should not give an almsbowl to anyone, nor should one receive an almsbowl from anyone;
one should not give a robe to anyone, nor should one receive a robe from anyone;
one should not give requisites to anyone, nor should one receive requisites from anyone.
One should not have one person’s hair cut, nor should one cause another person’s hair to be cut;
one should not perform service for one person, nor should one cause service to be performed by another;
one should not perform a personal task for one person, nor should one cause a personal task to be performed by another.
One should not act as another’s attendant, nor should one take on another as an attendant;
one should not have almsfood brought out for another, nor should one have almsfood brought out by another;
one should not enter a village without having asked permission from one’s teacher.
One should not go to a cemetery;
one should not depart for another region.
If the teacher is ill, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts, and one should wait for his recovery.
“This, monks, is the proper conduct for students toward their teachers, in which students should correctly conduct themselves toward their teachers.
Now at that time, the teachers were not conducting themselves properly toward their students.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these teachers not conduct themselves properly toward their pupils?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having had the community of monks assembled, questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that the teachers do not behave properly toward their pupils?
“It is true, Blessed One. …pe…
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, I shall lay down the proper conduct for preceptors toward their pupils, so that preceptors may behave correctly toward their pupils.”
“Monks, a teacher should behave properly toward his pupil.
In this regard, this is proper behavior:
a teacher, monks, should support and assist his pupil through recitation, interrogation, exhortation, and instruction.”
If the teacher has a bowl but the pupil does not have a bowl, the teacher should give his bowl to the pupil, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How can a bowl be obtained for the pupil?
If the teacher has a robe but the pupil does not have a robe, the teacher should give his robe to the pupil, or he should make an effort.
"How might a robe accrue to the pupil?
If the teacher has requisites but the pupil does not have requisites, the teacher should give requisites to the pupil, or he should make an effort:
"How might requisites accrue to the pupil?"
If the resident pupil is ill, having risen early, one should give him a tooth-stick, provide water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is rice gruel, one should wash the vessel and offer the gruel to him.
After he has drunk the gruel, one should give him water, receive the vessel, hold it low, and wash it carefully without clashing it against anything, then set it aside.
When the resident pupil has risen, the seat should be cleared away.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.

If the resident pupil wishes to enter the village, his lower robe should be given to him, his upper robe received back, and his waistband should be given to him. Having folded them, the outer robes should be given to him, and after washing it, the bowl with water for rinsing should be given to him.
Thinking, "He will turn back at this point," one should prepare a seat; water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone should be set out;
having gone out to meet him, one should receive his bowl and robe; an inner garment should be given to him, and his outer robe should be received.
If a robe is damp, it should be dried in the warmth for a short time, but the robe must not be placed directly in the heat.
The robe should be folded.
When folding the robe, one should fold it after turning back the edges by four finger-breadths.
"Lest there be a breakage in the middle," he said.
"The waist-band should be fastened around the body.
If there is almsfood and the resident pupil wishes to eat, one should give him water and then offer the almsfood."
The resident pupil should be asked for water.

After the teacher has finished eating, the pupil should give him water, receive the bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it, and let it warm for a short while in the heat; however, the bowl must not be left out in the heat.
The bowl and robes should then be put away.
When laying down the bowl...
[and so on] ...when laying down the robe...
having made a space from the edge of the robe toward the inside, the robe should be laid down.
When the resident pupil has risen, the seat should be removed; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper should be put away.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the resident pupil wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared.
If there is need for heat, heat should be prepared.
If the resident pupil wishes to enter the sauna, the powder should be kneaded and the clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench and going there, one should give the sauna-bench, receive the robe, and set it aside to one side;
then the bath-powder should be given and the clay should be given.
If one is able, one may enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover both the front and the back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior bhikkhus,
nor should one block the junior bhikkhus from their seats.
Service should be performed for the pupil in the sauna.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench and exit the sauna while shielding it from view both in front and behind.
Service should also be performed for the pupil in the water.
Having bathed first, the teacher should emerge from the water, dry his limbs, and put on his undergarment;
he should then wipe the water from the pupil’s limbs, give him his undergarment, and give him his upper robe.
Taking the sauna bench, he should return first and prepare a seat, as well as the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper.
The water for drinking should be set out, and the pupil should be asked whether he needs water.
If the dwelling where the pupil resides is dirty, it should be cleaned if he is able to do so.
When cleaning the dwelling, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side... [and so forth].
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water must be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
If dissatisfaction arises in the resident pupil, the teacher should dispel it himself, have it dispelled by another, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If remorse arises in the resident pupil, the teacher should remove it himself, have it removed by another, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a wrong view has arisen in a resident pupil, the teacher must resolve it, have it resolved, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a resident pupil has committed a heavy offense and deserves probation, the teacher must make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha grant probation to this resident pupil?"
If a pupil is deserving of being sent back to the beginning, the teacher must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha send the pupil back to the beginning?
If a pupil is deserving of the *mānatta* discipline, the teacher must make an effort...
"How indeed might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to the pupil?
If the pupil is worthy of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the teacher should make an effort:
"How indeed might the Saṅgha rehabilitate the pupil?"

If the Saṅgha intends to carry out a formal act against a resident pupil—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the teacher should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha refrain from carrying out this act against my resident pupil, or how can it transform it into something lighter?
Furthermore, once the Saṅgha has carried out the formal act against him—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the teacher should still make an effort.
"How might the pupil conduct himself properly, so that he performs his duties, sheds his hair, conducts himself to his own benefit, and the Saṅgha might settle this legal matter?
If the pupil’s robe needs washing, the teacher should instruct him,
"Wash it in this way," or he should make an effort, thinking, "How can the pupil’s robe be washed?"
If a robe must be made for a resident pupil, the teacher should instruct him, "Make it thus," or he should make an effort, thinking, "How can a robe be made for my resident pupil?
If dye must be boiled for a resident pupil, the teacher should instruct him, "Boil it thus."
Or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can I ensure that the dye for my pupil is prepared?
If the pupil’s robe needs dyeing, the teacher should instruct him:
"Dye it like this," or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can I ensure that my pupil’s robe is dyed?"
When dyeing a robe, it should be dyed by turning it over carefully again and again.
One must not leave while the drops of dye have not yet ceased.
If a resident pupil is ill, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts, and one should wait for his recovery.
"This, monks, is the proper conduct for teachers toward their pupils, as it should be correctly observed by teachers toward their pupils.
The Eighth Chapter on Conduct (Vattakkhandhaka). In this chapter there are nineteen matters and fourteen rules of conduct.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Those with sandals, those with umbrellas,
those with their heads covered, and those carrying water;

The virtuous abandon even a snake.
He cast off the umbrella from his shoulder and retreated.
Having set aside his bowl and robes,
and having been asked what is appropriate,
he should pour water from the washed [bowl].
Dry leather sandals;
an elder or a novice may ask about the place where one has stayed while wandering for alms.
The trainees, excrement, drinking water,
a pair of scissors, a mat, and then; time,

Remove the ground-covering rug.

the bed, the chair, and the spittoon.

and refuse used as a floor-covering—
A bed and chair for use,
a mattress, a sitting mat,

The bowl and robes, the ground,
the limit beyond and the limit within,
the eastern and the western.
The north and the south;
cold and heat, by day and by night;
the courtyard and the gateway.
The attendance hall, the fire-hall,
and the duties regarding the latrines; drinking water and water for washing.

Neither a seat nor water,
neither a footstool nor drinking water;
neither a salutation nor a prepared place—

having gone out to meet [the guest]..."
The sandals on one side,
the salutation, and the arrangement; the dwelling, the resort, and the training.
A place, water, and food;
a walking stick, a mat, and the time;
for one who is junior and seated.
One should pay homage and explain it;
one should apply the method just as it was below.
This has been pointed out by the Charioteer of the Dhamma.
This is the duty for those residing here:
departing monks and those carrying timber must open [the door] without asking.
The virtuous both take [the robes] and guard them,
and they express their disapproval [of misconduct].
Having settled the matter and secured [the robes],...
Having taken leave, one should depart—
whether a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera,
an ārāmika, or an upāsaka.
If he is able, he should exert effort to gather stones into a heap and set them in place.
And likewise in a place sheltered from rain.

and likewise in the open air.
Even if only his limbs remain,

Having abandoned four or five [of them],

they were unseemly and behaved in an improper manner.
There, in the matter of crowding in,
the new monks and the virtuous ones complained about the outer robe.
Having dressed the lower robe so that it covers the navel,
with the knot of the body’s virtues secured,
one should not expose what is concealed.
Well-restrained with upraised eyes;
upraised and loud laughter,
and the three kinds of swaying.
With shoulders covered, squatting,
well-restrained and with body concealed;
with eyes cast down, not laughing loudly, and not looking about.

leaning on [a pillar], covering oneself with the shoulder, and folding up the knees.

Having spread it out upon the water,
he lowered it and sprinkled [the water];
the outer robe was right there at its edge.
Regarding the rice and the bowl:
one should take the curry with the additional portion, and [the curry] should be level with all [the rice].
Mindfully and perceiving the bowl,
receiving the curry in proper sequence;
one should not cover it from a heap.
Perceiving the meditation as a formal intimation,
one whose hands reach everywhere should not speak at the door of the great circle.
Throwing up, cutting, and the boil;
shaking, and one who scatters rice;
and likewise, one who sticks out the tongue.
Chewing with a loud smacking sound;
licking the hands, the bowl, or the lips,
and receiving food with a hand that is already soiled.
As long as not all the water has been poured out by tilting [the vessel] low,
the outer robe remains clinging to its edge.
Having lowered it to the ground,
they return with the food still upon it,
their huts well-concealed.
This is the rule for the meal hall, established by the King of Dhamma:
those who are poorly dressed and lack decorum [should not enter].
And without careful observation, acting impulsively; too far away, too long, or too quickly—
likewise is the practice of one who wanders for alms.
One should walk with body concealed,
well-restrained, with eyes cast down;
avoiding loud laughter and noisy chatter.
And there are three ways of shaking:
leaning on a pillar, with the head covered, squatting,
and having observed [the object], doing so suddenly.
Far away, too long, or too quickly;
the seat, the ladle,
and the placing of the vessel.
Having raised [the bowl] and having set it down,
one should not look at the recipient;
it is the same regarding the curry as it is regarding the rice.
A bhikkhu should go covered by his outer robe,
walking with himself concealed,
restrained and with eyes cast downward.
Laughing loudly, and laughing with uplifted [shoulders];
being quiet, the three types of shaking,
[leaning] on the elbows, with head covered, and the cock-like [posture].
One who first offers a seat,
drinking water, and water for washing;
one may eat when invited later.
One should cause it to be immersed,
lift it out, settle it, sweep it,
and set it down empty and void.
One should not make gestures with the hands;
this is the rule for one who goes for alms.
One should not [use] water or fire.
Regarding constellations, directions, and thieves— having ground everything down with the thought "it does not exist," he then [placed] his robe on the edge of his bowl.
Now, having slung [the bowl] over the shoulder,
keeping the three circles perfectly round,
one should conduct oneself according to the practice for alms-gathering.
He went even into the forest.
Having placed his bowl on his shoulder, his robe on his head,
and having carried drinking water;
The fire for common use,
the fire-drills, and even a small axe;
a lunar mansion or its specific location.
One should also be skillful regarding the directions;
this is the conduct prescribed for forest-dwellers by the Supreme among Beings.
They sprinkled [water] in the open air,
and the virtuous ones complained:
"If the monastery is dirty..."
First, the bowl and robes;
then the mattress, the pillow, the bed, the bench, and the spittoon.
The walls were unplastered,
with corners blackened by red ocher;
heaps of refuse lay near the monks.
In a military camp, at a water source,
near a place for communal use,
in a place sheltered from the wind, and in an open courtyard.
A rug for the lower part, a foot-rest, and a bed;
a bench, a mattress, and a sitting mat.
The bowl, the leaning board,
the robe and alms-bowl, the ground,
the limit beyond and the enjoyment within.
To the east and to the west,
to the north and to the south;
in cold and heat, by day and by night.
The surrounding walkway and the gateway;
the attendance hall, the fire-hall, the restroom, and the drinking water shed.
The water-pot for rinsing, the elders,
the recitation, the questioning, and the study;
the Dhamma extinguishes the lamp.
Neither opening nor closing it,
he should not even let it touch his ear as he turns around when grown old.
The Great Hero prescribed that rule regarding dwellings;
even when being barred from the door, [they remained].
The virtuous ones, having fainted,
lie abandoned; one should discard the ashes and likewise the surrounding plaster.
The cell, the gatehouse, the hall,
the trough for powder and clay;
the entrance is not [directly] in front of the elders.
If he does not exert himself in a new [practice],
there will be a high road ahead,
mud, filth, and a stool.
Having extinguished [the fires] and closed [the door],
one should perform the duties in the sauna;
one should not fail to show respect according to seniority.
And in succession,
he suddenly expelled excrement, urine, and spittle, along with wood splinters and his own entrails.
The harsh well was suddenly uprooted by the monkey with his tail;
he coughed both inside and outside.
And while crossing a rope;
he suddenly lifted up one who was standing,
and [emitted] a sneeze, wood, and excrement.
Urine, saliva, and harsh words;
a well and a latrine-seat;
one should not lift these with excessive force.
One should not make a "capucapu" sound with one's sandals;
nor should one conceal what is not yet finished,
nor cover up what has already been removed.
The cowshed, the surrounding wall,
the courtyard, and the gateway;
the water for rinsing and the water [for washing].
The duty [is performed] in the toilet and the restroom.
Sandals, tooth-sticks,
water for rinsing the mouth, and a seat;
Having washed the gruel-water,
the scrapings, and the village [refuse];
the lower robes and the waistbands.
The bowl with its rim intact and water cleared out; afterwards,
the triple circle and the circular binding.
If, after washing [the bowl] while it still contains water,
one places it within arm's reach [of another] while speaking, there is an offense.
Having first arrived, [he offers] a seat,
water, a footstool, and a towel;
having gone out to meet him, [he offers] a lower robe.
One should place the bowl on a low stool;
one should eat while sitting on a spread of grass;
the drinking water should be kept at a low level.
One should not set down one’s bowl and robes for even a moment on the ground,
whether it be the far side or the near side of a boundary.
A water-drawing machine, a washing place,
a place for bathing, cold water, warm water, and a sauna.
Powder [should be applied] behind the clay.
A stool, a robe, powder,
and clay suffice for the face.
In front of the monastery,
at the boat, and at the preparatory rite;
when one has bathed in the water in front.
Having dressed the preceptor,
[he should provide] a lower robe and an upper robe,
as well as a bench and a seat.
The footstool, the bench, and the water-pot;
the indication of water and the inquiry;
one should thoroughly clean what has been soiled.
First, the bowl and robes;
the sitting mat and the rug,
and the mattress and the pillow.
A bed, a bench, a footstool,
a spittoon, and a backrest;
the ground, continuity, and light.
Yellow orpiment, black,
and unprepared [pigments]; floor-coverings, foot-wipers,
beds, stools, and pillows.
The sitting mat, spittle,
the back, the bowl, and the robe;
the eastern and the western [sides].
The north and the south,
cold and heat by day and night,
the surrounding cloister and the gatehouse.
The attendance hall, the fire-hall, the restroom, drinking water, and food;
the rinsing-water, and lack of delight.
Remorse and wrong view are heavy;
the root [offenses] are mānatta,
abbhāna, tajjanīya, and niyassaka.

a suspension, or a censure has been performed,

In the royal city, there was a redistribution:

The preliminary work, service,
the alms-round after [the meal], and entering [the village];
not [visiting] the charnel ground or the directions.
One should attend upon him for as long as life lasts;

Exhortation, recitation of the teachings,
questioning, and the bowl and robe;
requisites, and the sick.

One who is observant of the proper conduct toward co-residents,
likewise toward pupils,
and toward those who are newcomers;

the one at the head of the meal, and the one for the alms-gatherer.
Whatever duty there is in the forest dwellings,
and whatever in the monasteries;
in the sauna and the privy—
The duties toward a preceptor apply to a co-resident;
likewise, whatever duties apply toward teachers apply to a pupil.
There are nineteen matters in the *Vatta* section and fourteen in the *Khandhaka*.
One who does not fulfill the duty...
One does not fulfill virtue;
with impure virtue and poor wisdom,
one finds no one-pointedness of mind.
One whose mind is distracted and not one-pointed does not see the Dhamma correctly;
not seeing the true Dhamma, he...
One is not liberated from suffering.
While fulfilling the duties, one also fulfills virtuous conduct.
One whose virtue is purified and who possesses wisdom attains one-pointedness of mind;
with an undistracted mind, he is focused on a single object.
One who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight,
seeing the true Dhamma,
